turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.

Meredith stops just inside the door, still holding her bag, and doesn't sit.

"Hale. I have a call at 4:40, so let's use the time.

Owen found out about this zero from the gradebook, on his phone, in the middle of class. Who decided on it, and when was he asked for his side?"

Meredith sets her bag on the nearest desk and stays standing.

"Go ahead. I'm listening.

Before you do, I'll want whatever you're about to say in an email afterward, with dates. Start with the checker. What did it flag, and who looked at the flag before the zero went in?"
I'm getting dozens of these essays now. What would a fair process for catching AI writing look like? What would you put in the policy?

Meredith's mouth tightens slightly. She pulls out the chair at the desk and sits for the first time.

"You're asking me to draft your policy. Fine. I've read enough of them from the other side.

One: a detector score is never evidence. It's a reason to look. Software gets false positives, and you know that or you wouldn't be asking me.

Two: no grade change until the student has been told, in writing, what the concern is and what it's based on. Then he gets to answer. Zero second, never first.

Three: you need something besides the score. Drafts. Version history. Earlier writing samples. A conversation where the student explains his own argument. A kid who wrote it can talk about it.

Four: someone other than the flagging teacher reviews it. Someone who didn't raise the concern.

Five: a written finding, with a standard stated. Not 'it seemed off.'

Six: a deadline. Review in days, not months. Applications don't wait for appeals. I've seen what happens when they do.

Seven: nothing goes in a permanent file unless there's a finding after that process. And a flag that doesn't hold up gets removed.

Eight: private. Not a gradebook notification in the middle of class.

She holds your eye.

That's the policy. Now tell me which of those eight happened with Owen's essay. Take them in order."
